questions.stem: Thucydides says the ‘truest cause’ of the Peloponnesian War, though the least spoken of, was:
options: the Megarian Decree and Pericles' refusal to repeal it in 432
the Persian king's gold, which paid both sides to go to war
a quarrel between the kings of Sparta over the Spartan throne
the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta
questions.explanation: Thucydides separates the open grievances, such as Corcyra and Potidaea, from the underlying cause: Athens' rising power and the fear it produced in Sparta. He treats the Megarian Decree as one of the stated complaints, not the real cause.

questions.stem: In about 460 BCE, Megara left the Peloponnesian League and allied with Athens. According to Thucydides, this was the beginning of:
options: the Delian League, which Megara joined as its first member from the Peloponnese
the Thirty Years Peace, which made Megara a neutral city between the two sides
Corinth's bitter hatred of Athens, since Megara had been at war with Corinth
Sparta's alliance with Persia against the growing power of the Athenians
questions.explanation: Megara joined Athens because Corinth was pressing it in a border war, and Athens then held Megara's ports and built walls to Nisaea. Thucydides says Corinth's fierce hatred of Athens dated from this, which matters for the outbreak of war in 431.

questions.stem: Under the Thirty Years Peace of 446/5 BCE, Athens and Sparta agreed that:
options: the two cities would share command of a united fleet against Persia
each side kept its allies, and disputes would go to arbitration
Athens would dissolve its empire and free all its tributary allies
Sparta would pay Athens to withdraw from Boeotia and Megara
questions.explanation: The peace recognised the two blocs: neither was to take the other's allies, neutral states could join either side, and disputes were to be settled by arbitration. Athens gave up its holdings in the Megarid and the Peloponnese but kept its empire.

questions.stem: In 433 BCE Athens made only a defensive alliance with Corcyra, not a full alliance. Thucydides explains that the Athenians chose this because they:
options: wanted Corcyra's navy without openly breaking the Thirty Years Peace
feared Corcyra would use a full alliance to attack Athens' own colonies
had already promised Corinth that they would not fight against its fleet
hoped Sparta would join the alliance once Corcyra had defeated Corinth
questions.explanation: Corcyra had a large navy and lay on the route to Italy and Sicily, and the Athenians expected war with the Peloponnesians anyway. A defensive alliance let them help Corcyra if attacked while claiming they had not broken the peace, though their ships still fought Corinth at Sybota.

questions.stem: Potidaea was both a colony of Corinth and a tribute-paying member of the Athenian empire. In 432 BCE, Athens demanded that Potidaea:
options: join the Peloponnesian League and break all of its old ties with the city of Athens
hand over the Corinthian fleet sheltering in its harbour to the Athenian generals
pull down its sea wall, give hostages and send away its Corinthian magistrates
pay double tribute and accept an Athenian garrison on its acropolis for ten years
questions.explanation: Fearing revolt, Athens ordered Potidaea to demolish its wall on the Pallene side, give hostages and expel the magistrates Corinth sent each year. Potidaea revolted with Corinthian help, and the Athenian siege became another grievance for Corinth.

questions.stem: The Megarian Decree of about 432 BCE:
options: gave the Megarians Athenian citizenship in return for their help against Corinth
excluded Megarians from the harbours of the Athenian empire and the Attic market
made Megara a member of the Delian League and placed an Athenian garrison there
ordered the Megarians to destroy the walls that joined Megara to the port of Nisaea
questions.explanation: The decree was an economic sanction that cut Megara off from trade across the Athenian empire. Sparta later said war could be avoided if it were revoked.

questions.stem: Spartan envoys told Athens that war could be avoided if the Megarian Decree were revoked. In Thucydides, Pericles argues against giving way because:
options: yielding on a small demand would show fear and invite greater demands
the decree was a sacred law that only the gods could change or cancel
Megara had already agreed to rejoin the Delian League on Athens' terms
the ekklesia had no power to repeal a decree it had passed earlier
questions.explanation: Pericles tells the Athenians not to think they would be going to war over a trifle: giving in under threat would mark them as weak, and more demands would follow. He offered arbitration under the Thirty Years Peace instead.

questions.stem: At the Spartan assembly in 432 BCE, the Corinthian speakers urged Sparta to fight by:
options: offering Sparta the Corinthian fleet and the city of Potidaea
reporting that the Persian king had promised to pay for the war
reminding Sparta that it had lost to Athens at the Battle of Tanagra
contrasting restless, daring Athenians with slow, cautious Spartans
questions.explanation: In Thucydides the Corinthians describe the Athenians as always innovating and on the move while the Spartans hesitate, and they hint that they will seek other allies if Sparta does nothing. Sparta had in fact won at Tanagra in 457.

questions.stem: At the Spartan assembly in 432 BCE, King Archidamus urged delay, but the ephor Sthenelaidas called for war. What does this episode reveal about decision-making in Sparta?
options: the allies of the Peloponnesian League chose Sparta's ephors
the ephors could lead the assembly against the advice of a king
the kings alone decided on war, and the apella only advised them
the gerousia overruled the apella whenever it voted for war
questions.explanation: Sthenelaidas, an annually elected ephor, put the question and asked the Spartans to divide physically because he claimed he could not tell which shout was louder; most voted that Athens had broken the peace. A respected king's caution did not prevail.

questions.stem: Pericles' strategy at the start of the war was to:
options: invade the Peloponnese by land to free the helots from Sparta's rule
sail at once to Sicily to cut off the grain supply of the Peloponnese
bring the people inside the walls, avoid a land battle and use the navy
meet the Spartan army in a single great hoplite battle outside Athens
questions.explanation: Because Athens could not match Spartan hoplites but controlled the sea, Pericles relied on the Long Walls, imports by sea, the empire's revenue and naval raids on the Peloponnese, and warned against adding to the empire during the war. Thucydides presents this as the strategy his successors abandoned.

questions.stem: Which was a consequence of the plague in Athens in 430–429 BCE?
options: Pericles was fined and briefly deposed, and later died of the disease
Sparta made peace at once because its own army refused to enter Attica
the Athenians abandoned the city and moved to the island of Salamis
Cleon was exiled for proposing that the walls be opened to the sick
questions.explanation: The plague killed many Athenians crowded inside the walls, the Athenians sent envoys to Sparta without success, and they fined and removed Pericles before re-electing him; he died in 429. Thucydides also describes a collapse of respect for law and religion.

questions.stem: In the debate over Mytilene in 427 BCE, Diodotus persuaded the Athenians not to kill all the men of the city mainly by arguing that:
options: the decree was illegal because Cleon had proposed it without the boule
mass killing was against Athens' own interests and would make revolts harder to end
the Mytileneans were innocent and the gods would punish Athens for killing them
Sparta had promised to make peace if Athens spared the citizens of Mytilene
questions.explanation: Diodotus deliberately argued from expediency, not justice: if rebels expected death whatever they did, they would fight to the end, and Athens would lose the support of the common people in allied cities. A second trireme reached Mytilene just in time.

questions.stem: At Pylos in 425 BCE, Cleon promised to capture or kill the Spartans trapped on Sphacteria within 20 days. The outcome was significant because:
options: Athens lost its fleet, which forced it to agree to the Peace of Nicias
Spartiates surrendered, shocking Greece and giving Athens hostages
Cleon was killed and Nicias took over the command of the army
the Spartans escaped by sea and invaded Attica the same summer
questions.explanation: Cleon, with Demosthenes, kept his promise, and Spartan citizens surrendered rather than die, which astonished the Greeks. Athens threatened to kill the prisoners if Sparta invaded Attica again, so the invasions stopped while they were held.

questions.stem: In 424 BCE the Spartan Brasidas marched to Thrace and won over Amphipolis and other cities of the Athenian empire largely by:
options: offering them moderate terms and freedom from Athenian rule
bribing their generals with gold supplied by the Persian king
besieging each of them until its people were starved into surrender
landing a fleet in their harbours while the Athenian ships were away
questions.explanation: Brasidas presented Sparta as the liberator of the Greeks and gave Amphipolis generous terms, so it went over before Athenian help could arrive. His speed and persuasion struck at Athens' revenue and timber supplies in the north.

questions.stem: Thucydides was the Athenian general who failed to save Amphipolis in 424 BCE, and he was exiled for 20 years. How does this affect his value as a source?
options: it shows that he wrote his history while serving as a Spartan commander
exile let him gather information from both sides, though his own role needs scrutiny
it makes his whole history worthless, since he wrote it only to defend his own conduct
it means he could not have known anything about events in Athens after 424
questions.explanation: Thucydides says exile allowed him to observe both sides, especially the Peloponnesians, at leisure. His account of Amphipolis is brief and does not dwell on blame, so historians weigh his own role carefully while valuing his access.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Amphipolis in 422 BCE, both Cleon and Brasidas were killed. Thucydides says this made peace possible because:
options: neither city had any other general who could command an army
the gods were thought to have shown they wanted the war to end
their deaths left both cities without any money to keep fighting
they had been the leaders on each side most opposed to peace
questions.explanation: Thucydides presents Cleon and Brasidas as the chief opponents of peace, Brasidas for his glory and Cleon because war concealed his misdeeds. With them gone, Nicias and the Spartan king Pleistoanax negotiated the peace of 421.

questions.stem: The Peace of Nicias of 421 BCE failed to bring lasting peace mainly because:
options: Athens refused to return the Spartan prisoners taken at Sphacteria to their homes
Persia invaded Ionia within a year and forced both cities back into the war
Nicias was ostracised the following year and the treaty was cancelled at once
Corinth and Boeotia rejected it and some of its terms were never carried out
questions.explanation: Corinth, Boeotia, Megara and Elis refused to sign, and Amphipolis was never handed back to Athens, so tension continued. Athens did return the prisoners, and Nicias remained a leading general until his death in Sicily.

questions.stem: The Sicilian Expedition began in 415 BCE after an appeal for help from:
options: Corcyra, which feared an invasion from Sicily
Sparta, which asked Athens to defend the Greeks of Italy
Segesta, a Sicilian city at war with its neighbour Selinus
Syracuse, which wanted Athenian help against Carthage
questions.explanation: Segesta asked Athens for help against Selinus, which was backed by Syracuse, and fooled the Athenian envoys about its wealth with borrowed gold and silver vessels. Syracuse was the expedition's main enemy.

questions.stem: In the assembly debate of 415 BCE, Nicias tried to stop the Sicilian Expedition by:
options: exaggerating the size of force needed, which only made the Athenians keener
proposing that the generals be chosen by lot rather than by election
revealing that Alcibiades had been secretly in contact with the Spartans
threatening to resign his command unless the assembly voted for peace
questions.explanation: Nicias hoped a huge demand for ships, men and money would deter the Athenians, but they voted an even larger expedition. Thucydides presents this as a misjudgement that increased the scale of the later disaster.

questions.stem: After the mutilation of the Herms, Alcibiades was recalled from Sicily to stand trial and fled to Sparta. There, according to Thucydides, he advised the Spartans to:
options: invade Ionia and recover its cities from the Persian king
free the helots so they could serve as rowers in the fleet
send a commander to Syracuse and fortify Decelea in Attica
make peace with Athens and leave Sicily to the Athenians
questions.explanation: Alcibiades urged Sparta to send a Spartiate to lead the Syracusan resistance, which led to Gylippus's arrival, and to establish a permanent fort at Decelea. Both proposals did great damage to Athens.

questions.stem: In 413 BCE Nicias delayed the Athenian retreat from Syracuse because:
options: Demosthenes refused to leave until he had captured Epipolae
an eclipse of the moon occurred, and the seers advised waiting
the Spartan king Agis offered a truce while terms were drafted
Alcibiades returned to Sicily with orders from Athens to stay
questions.explanation: After the eclipse, the seers advised waiting thrice nine days, and the pious Nicias agreed, so the Syracusans were able to trap the fleet in the Great Harbour. Demosthenes, who had already failed in the night attack on Epipolae, wanted to leave at once.

questions.stem: Thucydides says Nicias least deserved his fate of all the Greeks of his time, because of his devotion to virtue. What does this judgement show about Thucydides' approach?
options: he could respect a man's character while showing his decisions led to disaster
he blamed the gods alone for the loss of the Athenian army and fleet in Sicily
he hid Nicias's mistakes because Nicias had been his commander
he believed that only pious men could be trusted with military command
questions.explanation: Thucydides shows Nicias's caution, his inflated request for forces and his delay after the eclipse contributing to defeat, yet admires his conduct of life. The judgement mixes personal sympathy with a critical narrative of his choices.

questions.stem: Looking back on the Sicilian Expedition, Thucydides argues that it failed less because of a misjudgement of the enemy than because:
options: the generals were chosen by lot and lacked any military experience
Persia paid the Syracusans to build a fleet larger than the Athenians'
those at home, absorbed in rivalry, failed to support the expedition
the Spartan hoplites were too strong for any Athenian army to defeat
questions.explanation: In his assessment of Pericles' successors, Thucydides blames private quarrels and the struggle for leadership, including the recall of Alcibiades, for undermining the expedition. Athens' generals were elected, not chosen by lot, and Persian money mattered later in the Aegean, not at Syracuse.

questions.stem: The Spartan fortification of Decelea in 413 BCE hurt Athens chiefly because:
options: it blocked the Hellespont and cut off the grain ships from the Black Sea
it gave Sparta a harbour from which to attack the Piraeus at night
it forced Athens to give up its alliance with Corcyra and Argos
it kept enemy troops in Attica all year, and many slaves deserted to them
questions.explanation: Unlike the yearly invasions, the fort at Decelea occupied Attica permanently, cutting Athens off from farms and the Laurion silver mines; Thucydides says more than 20,000 slaves deserted. The Hellespont route was cut later, after Aegospotami.

questions.stem: In the treaties of 412–411 BCE between Sparta and the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, Sparta:
options: allowed Persian troops to garrison Sparta while the army was abroad
accepted the King's claim to the Greek cities of Asia in return for funds
promised to hand Athens to the Persians once the war had been won
agreed to pay tribute to Persia from the profits of the Laurion mines
questions.explanation: Persian money for rowers was the price of recognising the King's rights over the Greek cities of Asia Minor, a reversal of the Persian War ideal of Greek freedom. It gave Sparta the means to build a fleet able to challenge Athens.

questions.stem: While living with Tissaphernes, Alcibiades advised the satrap to:
options: give Sparta all the money it asked for at once
invade Attica himself with an army from Sardis
make Alcibiades governor of the Greek cities of Ionia
let the Athenians and Spartans wear each other out
questions.explanation: Thucydides says Alcibiades told Tissaphernes it was in Persia's interest to keep both sides weak rather than help either to victory. He then used his supposed influence with Tissaphernes to bargain for his return to Athens.

questions.stem: The oligarchic revolution of 411 BCE in Athens was helped by:
options: a vote of the fleet at Samos to abolish the democracy in Athens
the death of every general in the plague that struck the city
a claim that Alcibiades could win Persian support if democracy were changed
a Spartan army that occupied Athens and appointed the Four Hundred to govern it
questions.explanation: Oligarchs argued that a government Persia could trust, with Alcibiades recalled, would bring Persian money, and the Four Hundred took control. The fleet at Samos stayed loyal to democracy and recalled Alcibiades as its general.

questions.stem: After his recall by the fleet, Alcibiades won victories such as Cyzicus in 410 BCE. He lost his command in 406 BCE because:
options: he refused to sail against Lysander, saying the fleet was too weak
his deputy lost the battle of Notium to Lysander while Alcibiades was away
he was convicted of profaning the Mysteries a second time on his return
he went over to the Spartans again and betrayed the fleet at Aegospotami
questions.explanation: Alcibiades left his helmsman Antiochus in charge with orders not to fight, but Antiochus engaged Lysander and was defeated. The Athenians blamed Alcibiades, did not re-elect him, and he withdrew to his strongholds in Thrace.

questions.stem: Lysander's friendship with Cyrus the Younger, son of the Persian king, mattered because Cyrus:
options: gave Lysander the throne of Sparta in place of King Agis
paid higher wages to Spartan rowers, drawing men away from the Athenian fleet
sent Persian infantry and archers to fight alongside the Spartans at Aegospotami
persuaded Tissaphernes to switch his support from Sparta to Athens
questions.explanation: Xenophon says Cyrus funded an increase in pay from three to four obols a day, which helped Lysander man his fleet and tempted rowers away from Athens. Persian money, not Persian troops, decided the naval war.

questions.stem: Lysander's victory at Aegospotami in 405 BCE was decisive because:
options: Athens lost nearly all its ships and so its grain route from the Black Sea
the Spartan king Agis was killed in the battle, which ended the occupation of Decelea
Persia was defeated in the battle and withdrew its support for Sparta
the Athenian army in Sicily was cut off and forced to surrender
questions.explanation: Lysander caught the Athenian fleet beached at the Hellespont and captured most of its ships, so Athens could no longer protect its grain supply and was besieged into surrender. The Sicilian disaster had happened eight years earlier.

questions.stem: When Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, the terms included that Athens would:
options: be destroyed and its people sold into slavery, as Corinth had demanded
pay Persia the tribute that the Delian League had collected since 478
hand over Attica to Thebes and move its citizens to the island of Salamis
pull down the Long Walls and Piraeus walls and give up all but 12 ships
questions.explanation: Xenophon reports that Athens had to demolish its walls, surrender its fleet except 12 ships, recall its exiles and follow Sparta's lead. Corinth and Thebes wanted Athens destroyed, but Sparta refused, citing Athens' service in the Persian Wars.

questions.stem: After the surrender of Athens, the Thirty Tyrants took power with the support of Lysander. Their rule ended in 403 BCE when:
options: the Persian king ordered Sparta to restore the Long Walls of Athens
democrats led by Thrasybulus fought back and democracy was restored
Lysander executed them and set up a board of ten Spartan harmosts
Alcibiades returned from Persia with an army and expelled them
questions.explanation: Thrasybulus and the exiled democrats seized Phyle and the Piraeus, and the Spartan king Pausanias, a rival of Lysander, allowed a settlement restoring democracy. Alcibiades had been killed in Phrygia in 404.

questions.stem: The Samians honoured Lysander as a god, and he installed boards of ten loyal men, backed by Spartan governors, in many former Athenian allies. These details suggest that:
options: Lysander's personal power had grown beyond what Sparta found comfortable
Sparta had become a democracy that worshipped its successful generals
Lysander had freed the Greek cities as Sparta had promised in 431
the Persian king had made Lysander satrap of the Greek cities of Asia
questions.explanation: Divine honours and networks of personal supporters made Lysander unusually powerful, and the Spartan authorities soon moved to limit him, for example when Pausanias undid his settlement at Athens. The decarchies also undermined Sparta's claim to be liberating the Greeks.

questions.stem: Pericles' family background included:
options: a Spartan mother and a father who had been tyrant of Athens before Cleisthenes
a father who was a tanner and a mother from a family of metics in the Piraeus
descent from the Pisistratids, who had ruled Athens as tyrants until 510
an Alcmaeonid mother, Agariste, and a father, Xanthippus, who commanded at Mycale
questions.explanation: Pericles' mother was a niece of Cleisthenes, linking him to the Alcmaeonids, and his father Xanthippus led the Athenians at Mycale in 479. The tanner's background belongs to Cleon, a later rival of the aristocratic leaders.

questions.stem: Which democratic reforms are associated with Pericles?
options: the creation of the ten new tribes and of the boule of 500 drawn from the demes
the cancellation of debts and the right of appeal to the people's court
the abolition of the boule and the election of all officials by lot
pay for jurors and a law limiting citizenship to children of two Athenians
questions.explanation: Pericles introduced pay for jurors in the popular courts and the citizenship law of 451/0 BCE. The ten tribes and the boule of 500 belong to Cleisthenes, and debt cancellation and the right of appeal to Solon.

questions.stem: Plutarch reports that Pericles' opponents attacked his building program, including the Parthenon, mainly because it:
options: was paid for with money from the allies' tribute
honoured Spartan gods rather than Athena
was built by Persian architects and craftsmen
left no room in Athens for the citizens' houses
questions.explanation: According to Plutarch, critics such as Thucydides son of Melesias said Athens was decking itself out with the allies' money; Pericles replied that the allies paid for protection and Athens provided it. The Parthenon honoured Athena, the city's patron.

questions.stem: Thucydides wrote that under Pericles, Athens was ‘in name a democracy, but in fact rule by the first citizen’. This judgement suggests that Pericles' power rested on:
options: his position as hereditary archon and head of the Areopagus
his repeated election as general and his influence over the assembly
a special law of the ekklesia that made him sole ruler for life
the support of a Spartan garrison placed in Athens after 446
questions.explanation: Pericles held no special office beyond being one of ten generals, but his repeated election and persuasive authority meant the assembly usually followed him. Thucydides contrasts this with the rivalry and demagoguery of his successors.

questions.stem: When the war began, Pericles told the Athenians that if Archidamus spared his estates while ravaging Attica, he would give them to the state. He did this because:
options: Archidamus was his guest-friend, and Pericles feared being suspected of collusion
he wanted to win the support of the Spartan king for a quick and favourable peace treaty
Athenian law required generals to give their land to the state in wartime
his estates had already been confiscated after he was ostracised in 443
questions.explanation: Pericles and Archidamus were linked by guest-friendship (xenia), so the Spartans might spare his land to make him look a traitor. By pledging it to the state, Pericles protected his standing with the Athenians.

questions.stem: Nicias was one of the wealthiest men in Athens. His wealth came largely from:
options: collecting the tribute of the allies as an Athenian treasurer
trading in grain from the Black Sea through the Hellespont
hiring out slaves to work in the silver mines at Laurion
owning the largest olive estates in the plain of Marathon
questions.explanation: Xenophon records that Nicias owned a thousand slaves whom he leased to a mining contractor at Laurion. His wealth funded lavish public and religious spending that built his reputation for piety and caution.

questions.stem: Alcibiades' background included:
options: exile from Athens as a child for the crimes of his father
birth in Sparta to an Athenian father and a Spartan mother
being brought up as a ward in the household of Pericles
service as a rower in the fleet after a childhood in poverty
questions.explanation: After his father Cleinias died at Coronea in 447, Alcibiades was raised as a ward of Pericles, a relative through his Alcmaeonid mother. He was rich, aristocratic and a follower of Socrates.

questions.stem: In the Funeral Oration reported by Thucydides, Pericles calls Athens:
options: the heir of the Persians
an education to Greece
a fortress of the gods
the servant of Sparta
questions.explanation: Pericles praises Athenian democracy, openness and culture, calling the city an education (or school) to Greece. The speech is Thucydides' version of what Pericles said at the public funeral in the winter of 431/0.

questions.stem: Thucydides says that in reporting speeches he kept as close as he could to the general sense of what was said, while making speakers say what the occasion required. Historians therefore treat the speeches as:
options: complete inventions that tell us nothing about what was actually argued
official records copied from the inscriptions set up by each city
reconstructions that may mix the speakers' arguments with his own analysis
word-for-word transcripts taken down by scribes in the assembly at the time
questions.explanation: By his own account the speeches are not verbatim but are grounded in what was said, so they are valuable but shaped by his interpretation. Treating them as either exact records or pure fiction ignores what he tells us about his method.

questions.stem: Thucydides calls Cleon ‘the most violent of the citizens’, and Aristophanes mocks him in his comedies. A historian assessing Cleon should note that:
options: both writers were Cleon's close friends, so their criticism must be accurate
Cleon wrote his own history, which confirms Thucydides' account in every detail
comedies were official records, so Aristophanes is the more reliable source
both sources were hostile, so Cleon's influence may be understated or distorted
questions.explanation: Thucydides, an aristocratic general exiled during Cleon's ascendancy, and Aristophanes, a comic poet whom Cleon had attacked, both had reasons to portray him badly. Cleon's real achievements, such as Pylos, should be weighed against this hostility.
